headline: US 10-year Treasury yield up ~70bp in six weeks to just under 5.3%, highest since 2002, driven by persistent inflation concerns, fiscal policy fears and investors demanding more duration premium
reasoning: Joe Unwin notes that the US 10-year Treasury yield, the benchmark global bond yield, has risen about 70 basis points in roughly six weeks to just under 5.3%, levels not seen since before the GFC in 2002. The rise has been global, with Australian 10-year yields at around 5.4% and European yields also spiking. Critically, these higher yields are not solely the result of rate hikes this year; bond markets are also pricing in persistent inflation, fiscal policy concerns and elevated government debt. Because every asset class must clear a higher hurdle to beat the risk-free rate, this repricing has valuation implications across equities, credit and other markets.
quote: the US 10 year treasury yield, which is really the benchmark global bond yield has risen about 70 basis points in the last 6 or so weeks. That's a massive rise. It's now sitting just under 5.3%, which is close to it's highest level since 2002. So these are levels we haven't been to for a very long time, since before the JFC. And it's happened globally as well. Like you said, the Australian 10 year yields about 5.4%. Big spike in yields in Europe. And it's important to note that these increased yields haven't just come from rate hikes this year. It's also because bond markets are pricing in persistent inflation concerns around fiscal policy and government debt like we've seen in Europe. And also just the fact that investors are demanding more yield for earning duration risk.

quote: I think when we're thinking about the Australian market and it's interest rate trajectory relative to other developed economies, it could be slightly different just because the Australian economy looks a little bit more fragile than for example, the US, which is quite resilient. So our economy, we've already had four rate hikes this year and we probably do have a bit more interest rate sensitivity than for example, the US. So it's reasonable to assume that our rate hiking cycle we're in now probably won't be as as strong As, for example, the US, because I think the US economy can weather higher for longer rates, whereas I'm not sure our economy will do it as well.
